**In Praise of Moss**

Nobody plants moss on purpose, or almost nobody. It arrives the way dust does, uninvited and patient, filling the cracks between bricks and softening the north side of trees. We mostly notice it when we're trying to get rid of it, scraping it off roofs or poisoning it out of lawns. But moss was here first. It crept onto land roughly 470 million years ago, before flowers, before trees, before anything had roots at all.

What I love about moss is how little it asks. It has no true roots, just threadlike anchors called rhizoids. It drinks through its leaves, directly from rain and fog. When water disappears, many species simply dry out and wait, brittle and brown, sometimes for years. Then a single rainstorm arrives and they turn green again within hours, as if nothing happened. Scientists once revived moss that had been frozen under Antarctic ice for over 1,500 years.

There's a lesson in that, though I hesitate to force one onto a plant. Still, it's hard not to admire something that survives not by fighting its circumstances but by pausing through them. Moss doesn't grow tall or bloom. It doesn't compete for sunlight with the oaks. It occupies the small, damp, overlooked places and makes them beautiful.

Get down close to a patch sometime, eye-level with it. It becomes a forest: tiny stalks, spore capsules like lanterns, whole communities of mites and tardigrades wandering through. An entire world, quietly thriving, just below our notice.
